Mob Avenges Murder by Triple Killing.
BARSTOW, Fla., May 20.—Following the murder of Barney Brown yesterday one white and two colored men were killed this morning. Randall conducted a disreputable place where negroes were guards. Last night, following an examination into the death of Brown, negroes taken in hand by armed men, confessed that Randall followed Brown and killed him. They were allowed to go.

At daybreak this morning a mob of 25 raided Randall's resort and 200 shots were exchanged. None of the attacking party was injured, but Randall and two negro companions were riddled with bullets.

amos-randall-mulberry-1903-05-20.A6:
TRIPLE LYNCHING IN FLORIDA.
ONE WHITE MAN AND TWO NE GROES SHOT DOWN.
They Were Implicated in the Murder of a White Man—Crime Inspired by a "Blind Tiger" Keeper, White, Who Feared Exposure—Mob of 100 Did It.
TAMPA, Fla., May 20.—At Mulberry, Polk county, twenty miles from Tampa, a mob of 100 unmasked men to-day avenged an assassination by shooting to death the three men implicated in the crime. Late on Monday night Barney Brown, 60 years old, a well-known resident of the county, was returning from Bartow to his home at Mulberry, and was waylaid and assassinated on the public road.

A load of buckshot entered his head. After shooting him the assassins cut his throat and that of his horse.

The crime was discovered about daybreak. The entire region was aroused and then began a search for the guilty men. Henry Golden, colored, was arrested on Tuesday night and confessed that he was one of the murderers. By this time a mob of 100, fully armed, had gathered.

Golden said that he had been employed to do the killing by Amos Randall, a white man who came here recently from Pennsylvania, but who has been conducting a "blind tiger" on the outskirts of Mulberry, the county being strictly prohibition.

Golden said that Randall had a grudge against Brown, who had threatened to expose him for his illegal sale of whiskey.

According to the agreement Golden said he and the white man waylaid Brown and shot him, but he denied cutting his throat.

The confession was made known to the mob, which clamored for Golden's life. The negro was dragged into the town square and shot to death. Meantime, Dan Kennedy, another negro, was caught. He refused to tell anything concerning the killing, although admitting that he knew all about it. Kennedy was tied to a tree and threatened with death if he did not confess.

"If you want anything out of me you will have to shoot it out," he said.

At this a signal was given and more than 150 bullets were fired into Kennedy's body. It was so riddled that it slipped from the ropes which bound it to the tree, and fell to the ground.

The mob then started for the house of Randall, the white man. He was asleep, and in bed with him was Charles Jacobe, a drummer representing Charles Blum, a wholesale whiskey dealer of Jacksonville, Fla. The mob surrounded the house and at a signa' fired a volley into it.

One charge of buckshot splintered the headpiece of the bed on which the two men were sleeping. They jumped out of bed and ran from the house in their night clothes, Randall taking his rifle with him. The members of the mob recognized Randall as he ran. At once a hail of lead was directed at him and he was brought down, but had strength enough to crawl under a church building, where he died in a few seconds.

His body was dragged from under the church and riddled with bullets, every man in the mob taking a shot at it. The drummer, Jacobs, fled in another direction.

The three bodies were then taken to the public square and exhibited to the crowds who came in during the morning from all parts of the county. The members of the mob made no effort at concealing their identity, but remained in town all day.

Two hours after the killing had been done, Sheriff Tillis arrived from Bartow with a posse, and a Coroner's inquest was held. The jury rendered a verdict that Amos Randall, Henry Golden and Dan Kennedy came to their deaths from gun-shot wounds "at the hands of persons unknown." The Sheriff took charge of the bodies, and they were buried at noon without religious services.

As a result of the triple killing nearly every negro in the vicinity of Mulberry has disappeared and the phosphate mines are unable to operate. Jacobs after several hours' hiding in the woods, being unaware of the cause of the trouble and fearing that the mob was after him because of the unpopularity of whiskey men in a dry county, made his way to Bartow, where he learned the facts. The men composing the mob were leading citizens of the county including several State and county officials.

THREE LYNCHED NEAR TAMPA
One was White and Employ Negroes to Murder His Enemy.
(By Associated Press.)

BARTOW, FLA., May 20.—Following the murder of Barney Brown, reported yesterday, three men were shot to death this morning, about daylight at Mulberry, a phosphate town eight miles west of Bartow.

The dead are: Amos Randall, white, and Don Kennedy and Henry Goulding, colored, guards about the former's premises.

The negroes were questioned before Justice Cains court concerning the death of Brown. Their professed ignorance of the crime was not believed, and they were taken out into the darkness by an armed crowd which demanded the truth.

Goulding then broke down and told how Amos Randall had followed Barney Brown down the road Monday night and shot him through the head. There were probably twenty-five men in the mob that raided Randall's bar this morning, and perhaps two hundred shots altogether were fired. The bodies of the three men were literally riddled with bullets. Randall returned fire, but so far as known Justice Cain's court concerning the death without effect. Sheriff Tillis took charge of the bodies and had them buried. In all probability no arrests will be made. Fully half a car load of whiskey was seized by the officers in Randall's store. Randall came to this country several years ago from Pennsylvania, from where it is said he has a wife and daughter.

TWO LYNCHINGS.
Four Men Die at the Hands of Two Mobs.

Wash W. Jarvis, white, who, on Sunday, May 10, murdered his cousin, John Waldorp in Madison county, was taken from jail by a mob of citizens Tuesday night last, and lynched. Jarvis was said to have committed another murder about a year ago. Lawyers were about to secure his release on bond, and that fact probably caused the lynching.

ANOTHER LYNCHING.

Another lynching, which sent one white man and two negroes into eternity, occurred near Lakeland Wednesday.

Early Wednesday morning a white man named Barney Brown was waylaid and murdered about two miles from Bartow by Aleck Kennedy and Henry Golden, negroes, and when arrested they confessed to the murder and said they were hired to do so by a white man named Randall, who had just served a sentence in the chaingang for conducting a blind tiger at Mulberry. The three men were lynched on the same tree and at the same time. They were left hanging—the white man between the two negroes.

It is believed that Randall had Brown murdered because of information furnished against him (Randall) in his blind tiger business. It is regretable that this lynching occurred, but it shows what public sentiment is in Polk county in regard to the blind tiger business, and in this way may result in good.

THE STORY OF A CRIME
The assassination last week of a white man named Barney Brown and the subsequent lynching of another white man and two negroes at Mulberry, in Polk county, is directly traceable to the rum question. Polk county was in the throes of a "wet or dry" election, and Barney Brown was a very active worker on the anti-whisky side. The night before the election Mr. Brown was waylaid and shot to death on the highway.

This foul deed aroused strong and bitter feeling against the whisky element to whom was attributed the crime. Those who were undecided on the "wet or dry" question—on the fence, so to speak, got down on the "dry" side and carried the county against whisky.

The election over, the people of Mulberry began to hunt for the assassins of Mr. Brown. They soon struck a trail, and in a few hours they had a suspected negro under arrest. He broke down and confessed that he and another negro had committed the crime. He said they were bribed to commit the deed by one Amos Randall, a white man who ostensibly kept a grocery store, but whose real business was the illicit whisky traffic. He kept what is termed "a blind tiger."

A mob was soon formed. They lynched the negroes and then went after Randall. He lived a bachelor life in his rum den, and on the night of the occurrence, he had a guest in the person of Joe Jacobs, a whisky salesman for a Jacksonville house. Jacobs is well known all over the State, and is said to have practically a monopoly of the "blind tiger" trade in central and southern Florida.

He was here last Tuesday, and told the writer his experiences that night at Mulberry when Randall was lynched.

"First, I want to say," remarked Mr. Jacobs, "the account of the affair given in the Tampa Tribune is all wrong in so far as it relates to me.

"I went to Mulberry on the day of the election because I had been assured by Randall that everything was going to be "wet" by a large majority, and Randall was going to open a saloon right away, and promised me the order for the stock. That's how I came to be there.

"Well, the night before the election Brown was killed, and that caused an unusual amount of hard feeling, because people thought the "tiger men" had a lot to do with it; and then men who were "wet" dead easy turned round and voted the "dry" ticket. That's why the county went "dry."

"When it was all over, of course the "wets" were pretty blue, and I got ready to leave for Bartow. Randall begged me to stay all night with him. I refused at first, but he begged so hard, and had always been a good customer of mine, and
I was tired, so decided to stay. I had no
idea that he was capable of such a crime,
and had always found him straight. I
now believe that he was expecting some
sort of trouble that night and thought I
would be some sort of protection to him.
It was the first time he ever asked me to
stay all night with him.

"The mob came just about daybreak.
I was awakened by a volley of shotguns.
Before I could realize the situation, they
fired another volley through the side of
the house. The headboard of the bed we
lay upon was literally shattered, and the
splinters fell all over my face. My coat
and vest were hanging on the wall, and
were pierced by a dozen buckshot. For
a time we did not move. Finally the
firing ceased, and we heard the crowd
moving off up the street.

"Then we got up and dressed. I asked
Kandall what it all meant. He said he
did not know, but supposed they were
after him. Randall was cool and gritty.
He took his gun and went out the front
door, saying:

"'I'll die game if they come for me again.'

"That was the last I saw of him. I left
the place by a side door, went down an
unfrequented street into the main part of
the town. By this time it was daylight,
and I found a man opening his store. I
went in and told him what had occurred. His wife came in and gave me a cup of hot coffee. It revived me wonderfully.

"Shortly after escaping from Randall's house, the shooting broke out again be yond the house from where I was. That was when they killed Randall. I did not see the killing, nor did I see the mob. I heard them, and smelled the powder and shot. That was more than enough for me. After the excitement had died out a little, I got two men to go with me back to the Randall house, where I had left my sample case. As soon as I got that I made all possible speed for Bartow.

"When I got there I went to a hotel, and tried to collect my senses. I had not exactly lost them, but I confess that I was badly rattled. I do not believe that the mob knew I was in that house, and I do not think any of them would harm me knowingly, but I had miraculously escaped death, and the thought of it excited me. At the time I was tolerably cool, and dressed myself carefully before leaving Randall's house—even tied my neck-tie carefully.

CROWD CRIED "LYNCH NIGGER" Crowd Wanted to String Up Chap Who Cut Rowan. START ROUGH-HOUSE In Saloon Over a. Sand- wich and a Little Beer. NEGRO ARRESTED
Moundsville was the scene of a nasty cutting affray about five o'clock Saturday evening. Pat Rowan, a well known painter, of the above city, was cut across the left side, just above the abdomen and also across the right arm by Arthur Reese, a negro coal miner.

The trouble started in the Arlington saloon on Laffayette avenue. Some claim that it was done inside the saloon while others say it was done on the sidewalk in front of the saloon. Pat Rowan and his brother, Jack Rowan, Arthur Reese and a large number of others were in the saloon at the time, and it is said Jack Rowan treated the crowd.

Reese took advantage of the occasion and got a glass of beer. He then fished a nickle from one of his pockets and purchased a sandwich. Some one in the crowd either purposely or accidentally knocked the sandwich from his hand, while others kicked it about the floor. Reese, who has a bad temper, and enjoys the reputation of being a dangerous colored man, became infuriated and the row started.

A few minutes later Pat Rowan either walked, or was pushed outside of the door and in an instant was followed by Reese, who was ejected bodily from the bar room. He landed on the outside on all fours, with an open knife in his hand.

Several persons on the outside say that Reese and another negro then started down the avenue. A moment later Jack Rowan came out and Pat said to him "See what the nigger done Jack', exhibiting the cut.

Jack started after Reese and soon overhauled him. A fight ensued and Rowan, although much the lighter in in weight of the two men, used his fist with good effect and unassisted conveyed the negro to the Mayor's office.

A large crowd soon collected in the office and things looked squally for a while and numerous cries of "Lynch the nigger" were heard, much to the discomfort of Reese, who trembled until his teenth chattered. Fortunately not attempt at lynching was made and Reese was hustled off to jail and will be given a hearing Monday.

Jack Rowan, who is a popular barber, employed in Hood's barber shap and who bears an excellent reputation, was infuriated over the dastardly assault made upon his brother and after Reese had been landed in the Mayor's office, he left the room, secured a pistol and was returning with the intention of shooting Reese, but was stopped by cooler heads, who took the pistol from him.

A man who gave his name as John A. Shaffer says he was standing in front of the saloon with Pat Rowan when Reese came up to Rowan and cut him. The wound is an ugly one, but is not thought to be dangerous. Dr. Houston dressed the wound and Rowan was able to go about a few hours later.

THE REIGN OF THE LIAR
He Is Injuring the Town and Inciting to Mob Violence.

The spirit of old Ananias is abroad in Daytona, and the healthy and limitless methods by which it is keeping up the old sinner's reputation as a monumental liar is working harm—producing a state of chronic alarm that may ultimately lead to serious consequences.

Lately several depredations have been committed in and around the city by a lawless element that is a part and parcel of almost every community, no matter how efficient its police regulations.

One lady has been outraged by a black brute, who is now in jail. Another has been knocked senseless on the street by a villian as yet unknown, while a third has been wontonly insulted on the main street and in the center of the business section of the town by a burly negro who was allowed to go scot free on the alibi testimony of members of his own family in the face of his positive identification by the lady he had insulted.

These are facts known throughout the city to every intelligent man, woman and child, and in the light of them, it is not a matter of much wonder that there is a feverish state of excitement in the public mind and a sense of dread and fear in the hearts of the women and children.

This condition, however, furnishes no excuse or palliation for the evil influences of the sensation mongers and calamity liars who are exciting and terrifying the community by exaggerating the crimes already committed and inventing others by inexcusable lying. There ought to be some way to get at all such characters and punish them, and we believe it could be done under the statute relating to malicious mischief.

A case in point occurred last Sunday afternoon, and came near precipitating mob violence over on the peninsula. A young lady, the daughter of E. A. Branch, of Goodall, was walking along the road, in a lonely place, when a negro suddenly appeared on a bicycle, riding toward her. When within a few yards of her the negro suddenly stopped, dismounted from his wheel and stood in an attitude of waiting. Such unusual conduct very naturecited alarm in the lady's mind, and she also stopped. The negro called to her to "come on." She turned and fled screaming to the nearest house, while the negro remounted his wheel and disappeared.

Why that negro stopped and waited for the lady, is known only to himself. His actions were well calculated to alarm her, for it is not a custom here for persons riding bicycles to halt on the highway for people on foot to pass them, on the contrary, it is the pedestrian who has to stand aside for the wheelman.
The news of the occurrence soon spread to this side of the river, and the tide of popular excitement, already stirred up by previous outrages, soon rose to feverish heights. Sheriff Turner, City Marshal Zuber, and a large number of citizens at once hurried across the South bridge to the peninsula on a man hunt.

The sheriff and the marshal did all they could to allay the excitement, but open threats of lynching were heard as the excited crowd spread across the wooded strip of land between the river and the ocean. Every bridge and avenue of escape from the peninsula was watched, but the negro could not be found. One suspect was arrested and taken before the lady, but she said he was the wrong man. He was released at once.

In the meantime, the liar was abroad, adding fuel to the smouldering tame in the popular mind. First came a rumor that two other ladies had been held up and robbed by, presumably, the same negro. This was followed by another rumor that a negro had thrown a lady into the Halifax river.

These rumors were groundless lies, the inventions of some evil, sinister genius, with some diabolical end in view. They soon took the wings of the morning, and spread over the city like a prairie fire, and if the negro who accosted Miss Branch had have been arrested that evening and identified by her, all the sheriffs and marshals on the East Coast could not have saved his neck. The city marshal informs us that the report circulated recently to the effect that Major Pellett was held up and robbed by two negroes was purely a fiction.

Vicksburg, Miss., July 7.—Just as the sun went down today, Cato Garrett, the 17-year-old negro boy who on last Saturday morning stabbed Harry Stout in the heart, inflicting a death wound, paid the penalty of his crime at the end of a rope.

He was jerked to eternity by a mob of fifteen determined men of Warren county, who entered the incoming Yazoo & Mississippi Valley passenger train and took their man from Officer Paul, who was conveying him here for trial tomorrow.

Garrett was hanged to a little country road bridge, east of the railroad, and not a shot was fired at the execution.

This morning the grand jury, which was specially convened by Judge Anderson to give Garrett a hasty trial, indicted Garrett, and Sheriff Brennan at once wired to Natchez, where Garrett was taken for safekeeping Saturday, to have him brought here this afternoon.

Sheriff Brennan and a posse were at the depot to meet the train, and were given the information by Officer Paul, who had accompanied Garrett, that the mob had taken his prisoner. Officer Paul reported that the men were all masked, had revolvers, and he was unable to resist.

Garrett Prays.

Just as the train bearing Garrett neared Stout's crossing, which is four miles south of this city, he cried: "Oh, Lord, there is where I killed him, and there is my brother in the field plowing."

Garrett was said to have prayed then and was in the act of praying when he was taken from the train by the mob, his neck being placed in the moose before he left the train.

Harry Stout was a popular young planter, well connected with the best people in the county, and since his murder there has been great feeling against his slayer.

Judge Anderson did all in his power to hasten the trial, but the close friends of the murdered man wanted to have quicker justice done.

HOWELL CITIZENS RAGE BLACK MAN IN CONDUCTOR'S UNIFORM EXCITES INDIGNATION. Negroes Severely Beaten-Women Start Aggressive Fight-Stricken on Eve of His Wedding.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

EVANSVILLE, Ind., June 16.—The color line was drawn at Howell, a railroad station two miles below here, this afternoon. The Evansville Street Car Company, whose line extends there, has been doing some repairing to the track and the passengers are transferred at the edge of town to another car that runs into the heart of the city. A negro was on the car as a conductor and late this afternoon a crowd of angry citizens surrounded the car and forced him to leave. It is said he will be made to leave the town. The citizens took charge of the car and brought it to the edge of the city, where a white conductor was given charge. For several years the sentiment against the negroes in Howell has been intense.

Three negroes were found in the railroad yards at Howell late to-night by a posse of citizens, and after being given a severe beating were forced to leave town at the points of revolvers. They were badly bruised and could hardly walk. The names of the negroes could not be learned. The citizens are greatly excited since the streetcar affair this afternoon and declare no negro shall remain in the place.

Men of Howells, Ind., Drive All Negroes Out of Town.
INDIANAPOLIS, June 17.—When the Interurban car from Evansville to Howells reached the latter place last night and was found to be in charge of a negro conductor named George Jerome, a dozen angry men boarded the car and gave him an unmerciful beating. They ordered him not to attempt to run a car into the town again.

Jerome was not accused of any offence, but was glad to give up his job. The company says it will not employ negro conductors again.

The beating of the negro created great excitement and men patrolled the streets declaring war on the colored race. Near midnight three other negroes were found hidden in the railroad yards and they were set upon, and all of them more or less injured with stones and sticks in the hands of the whites.

The people seemed beside themselves with rage, but no one could assign any reason, except that no negroes were wanted in the town. Two families of colored people living in the outskirts of the town fled.

THE NEGRO IN THE NORTH.
THE NEGRO IN THE NORTH.

The negro must begin to realize that if he lives in peace and quiet, and follows any business or calling for a living, the South is the place for him. Here he is among his real friends, and here he can labor unmolested and make an honest livelihood. Those at the North who have been so profuse with their professions of friendship for the negro, who have offered him a peaceful home among them and who have said so many hard thing of the South as to its treatment of the negro, have not protected him when he has left his home in the South and settled among them. They have not only failed to give him employment, but they have failed to protect him at his labor when employment has been given him. This is clearly shown by the treatment a colored man received the other day at Howells, Indiana, which was told by a special in the New York Sun from Indianapolis, as follows:

When the interurban car from Evansville to Howells reached the latter place last night and was found to be in charge of a negro conductor named George Jerome, a dozen armed men boarded the car and gave him an unmerciful beating. They ordered him not to attempt to run a car into the town again.

Jerome was not accused of any offense, but was glad to give up his job. The company says it will not employ negro conductors again.

The beating of the negro created great excitement and men patrolled the streets declaring war on the colored race. Near midnight three other negroes were found hidden in the railroad yards and they were set upon, and all of them more or less injured with stones and sticks in the hands of the whites.

The people seemed beside themselves with rage, but no one could assign any reason, except that no negroes were wanted in the town.

We have had no such treatment of the negro in the South as we have in the above account. It is true we have had no negro conductors of cars, but if we did, the public would not resort to violence; their protest would be shown only in declining to ride on that particular car so long as it was managed by a colored conductor. In the South the negro is employed, not only as a farm hand, but as school teachers of their own color, carpenter, brick-mason, blacksmith. wheelwright, teamster, house servants, cooks, butlers, nurses, and for almost any kind of work the whites have to do, and when they prove faithful and efficient they are well paid and protected. That is not the case in the instance above cited. Jerome had done no harm, yet he was unmercifully beaten because he had accepted the place of conductor.

The other three negroes were brutally beaten for no other reason than that they were colored. The colored population of the town was given notice to leave the town because no negroes were wanted there. But this is not the worst. The colored man must not only notice this treatment of his race in a Northern State, with surprise, but he must witness the lynching of members of his race in Indiana and Illinois by hanging and shooting for slight offences, which in the most lawless part of the South—if we have in lawless places—would be punished by the courts of the land. And added to these horrors, Wilmington, Delaware, now startles the country with the intelligence that a mob of two thousand men took the negro White from the work-house, where he was lodged for safe keeping, and burned him at the stake, after which his body was riddled with bullets.

Thus the colored man will see that negros are shot, hung and burnt in the North for offences, if committed in the South where he was raised, he would have courts to mete out justice to him and able counsel to defend him. He will also see that his race is denied the privilege of laboring in some localities in the North, whereas in the South he is as free to labor as the white man and is protected in his labor.

NEGRO LYNCHED BY CLARENDON MOB.
Sheriff Thought He Had Outwitted Mob but a Second Division Found Negro Who Was Forthwith Lynched.
Clarendon, June 25.—Shortly after midnight last night a mob of about fifty men called at the residence of Deputy Sheriff John Black and demanded the keys to the jail. The men are supposed to have been the friends and neighbors of John Coburn, the white man who sustained serious injuries at the hands of a negro named Jack Harris.

Sheriff Milwee readily agreed to let them into the jail and led the way, requesting them to choose a committee who should search the jail for the negro.

Mr. Milwee congratulated himself that he had outwitted the mob; for, fearing that something like a lynching would be attempted, he had given the negro into the custody of William Swift. Mr. Swift had conducted the prisoner to a barn that Sheriff Milwee had just built and there they were, in fancied security, while the mob were going through the jail. But it is now known that while the larger part of the mob were making this advance on the jail, another part were hot on the trail of the negro and his guard. It is not known how they knew the whereabouts of the men, but about the time the larger body of men were cursing their luck and departing from the jail, apparently convinced that they could not secure their man, that night at least, the other party had found Mr. Swift and his prisoner, had furnished good proof that it would be useless to try to save the negro, and were leading him away to find a convenient place to string him up.

Mr. Swift, whom the mob kept with them till after the job was finished, says that the crowd was orderly, there being no one under the influence of drink. The negro was allowed to pray, but was stopped when he got too loud.

The first trial at hanging was a failure, as the rope seems to have given way when the buggy in which the negro was standing was driven from under him. The next time he was drawn up by hand, and died from strangulation, his neck not being broken.

Probably such severe measures would not have been adopted with Harris had the mob not failed in its attempt to lynch the negro, Riley Park, who killed a white man named Fowler in the same neighborhood in which Mr. Coburn lives. This killing occurred a short time ago, and Sheriff Milwee was forced to send Park to the penitentiary for safekeeping. Since then the negroes are said to have grown very insolent in the Coburn neighborhood. The affair is deplored by many citizens here.

Jack Harris, colored, was hanged by a mob to the rafter in a wagon yard at Clarendon. FRIGHTENED NEGROES THREATEN EXODUS.
Clarendon, July 1.—The troubles out in the Fowler-Coburn neighborhood, beginning with the killing of Fowler and culminating with the lynching of Harris, the assailant of Coburn, have now developed a financial side. The negroes of that neighborhood have received anonymous letters setting forth that "the quickest way out of the country was the best," and a general exodus of negroes seemed imminent.

Most of the plantations in the disturbed district are the property of men residing in this city. Hearing that they were likely to be deprived of their black labor through the intimidation of unknown parties a number of them went out to the fearridden community yesterday afternoon with the hope of quieting the fears of the negroes and persuading them to remain on the places. On promise of protection from their landlords and the best citizens of that section, the darkies have consented to stay. The owners of the farms worked by the frightened blacks were much concerned because of the considerable loss their leaving would have occasioned.

It is generally believed that the intimidatory letters were the work of some irresponsible white renters who hoped, by producing a scarcity of labor, to cheapen rents. The better class of white farmers are anxious to have order restored and are sorry that a few reckless ones should earn for the community a reputation for lawlessness.

Four Negroes Under Arrest in Hagerstown, Md., and the Citizens Excited.

HAGERSTOWN, Md., Dec. 5.—Hagerstown is excited to-day over the arrest of four negroes who are charged with enticing young white girls under 18 years old. The arrests are the result of an investigation made yesterday afternoon by Justice Hoffman, upon the suggestion of State's Attorney Poffenberger.

Amelia S. Little, the seventeen year old white girl who was committed to the house of refuge for going with two negroes, William and Frank Keys, brothers, made a confession in which she involved three other white women, one the daughter of a well known citizen of Hagerstown.

Tyler, a negro cabman, and Mrs. May, are accused of arranging meetings between the negro men and the girls. Six or eight prisoners in jail who are alleged to have heard Miss Little make a confession testified at the investigation. William Keys left town before the officers could catch him. A small group of indignant men from Port Norfolk appeared at the county jail in Portsmouth very early yesterday morning, and demanded that the jailer surrender George Washington, the negro charged with attempting to assault four-year-old Marie Mason, daughter of Bruce Mason, a prominent Port Norfolk man. Fourteen years ago eight negroes were taken from jail in Barnwell, S. C., and hanged. They were accused of murder. The jail was not stoutly defended, and the officials were severely criticised. Saturday evening a Fourth of July dance was given at the village of Kline, and the country belles and beaux from miles around participated. A pistol flashed, and Sanders fell shot through the body. His friends were threatening, and Moore hurried across country to Barnwell, where he surrendered to Sheriff Louis Creech and was locked safely in jail. The sheriff had to leave Barnwell Monday night, and as he occupies rooms adjoining the jail, he gave the keys to his eighteen-year-old daughter, the only adult in his house. Late in the night there was a knock on the door. Miss Creech opened it, and was confronted by a body of masked men, the spokesman demanding the keys of the jail, saying they had come for Moore. The girl replied readily that she would get them from her father's room. She disappeared for a moment, returning with a repeating rifle to her shoulder, with finger on trigger. Mr. Ritchie, of New York; Ella Lowe, John Z., Jr., Jenkins and Hyslop. Mrs. Lowe was Miss Ella Jenkins, the daughter of Mrs. James by a former marriage. The obdy was received here on the noon train of the Norfolk and Southern Road, and sent to the residence of Lee Wood Walker, Portsmouth, the son-in-law of the deceased. The funeral will take place from the residence there to-morrow.

Mrs. Lowe was the half-sister of Mr. Edward S. James, chief clerk at the Monticello Hotel, and Mrs. S. M. Eley, of East Orange, N. J.

ELISON AND MOORE CASE.

The papers for the settlement of the difficult case of Ellison and Moore, of Hampton, were completed here to-day by S. Gordon Cumming and Judge Dudley, both of Hampton, and attorneys in the case in bankruptcy in the United States District Court. They will be held for the approval of Judge Waddill, who will hold court here to-morrow. The creditors of the firm are striving to have all of the property of both partners used for the settlement of the debts of the firm.

UNDER THE MANN LAW.

George W. Rappold, white, charged with selling liquor on Sunday, was fined $500 and costs and sentenced to sixty days in jail by Police Justice Taylor to-day. On a second charge of selling liquor without license, Rappold was fined $10 and costs and given six months in jail. Most of the witnesses were sailors and marines, who testified positively that they had bought liquor there yesterday.

Rappold made no defense and was not represented by attorney. Justice Taylor stated in court that he had received many personal complaints about the place, as a "blind tiger."

MONITOR ARKANSAS.

The monitor Arkansas arrived at the navy yard to-day. Her turret is to be repaired. It suffered from the same sort of weakness as that displayed by the Nevada. Her turret was broken loose by the recoil from the fire of twelve-inch guns simultaneously. The turret and the guns will be removed, as those of the sister monitor, still here. Tremendous cranes were prepared for the purpose.

Emmett R. Drary, while bathing in Elizabeth River late this afternoon, got into a hole beyond his depth and was drowned. His body was found and sent to his home. He was twenty-two years old and unmarried.
john-edwards-portsmouth-1903-07.A6:
WON SUIT FOR DAMAGES
Mrs. Laura Carr Was Awarded $4,000 by Judge Waddill
SENT TO PENITENTIARY
Negro Who Assaulted Four-Year-Old Child Was Not Given Death Penalty in Portsmouth—Narrow Escape from Drowning.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.) BEOLK VA July 28 Judge Wad

NORFOLK, VA., July 28.—Judge Waddill, of the United States District Court, awarded Mrs. Laura Carr $4,000. The suit was a libel on the ferry steamer City of Portsmouth for personal injuries. She sued for $20,000 on account of an accident in getting off the boat in June, 1902. Her ankle was crushed between the float and the steamer, and the fall which ensued broke the end of her spine. The plaintiff alleged that she was permanently injured, and the defendant contended that she came home late at night from a dinner and was not as alert to the rules for the safety of passengers as she might have been. The defendant will take an appeal.

John Edwards, colored, is on trial in Portsmouth for a criminal assault on a negro girl, Ada Wright, eleven years old. George Washington Griggs, whose punishment was fixed at eighteen years in the penitentiary by the same court yesterday for an assault on a four-year-old white girl, asks for a new trial. There were threats of lynching for both of these negroes, but the promise of speedy trials averted violence.

COLORED REFORM SCHOOL.

John Henry Smith, manager of the Virginia Manual Labor Society, which has a school in Hanover, was here to-day. He took the little negro boy, Lovely Young, sent to the school by Judge Hanckel, of the Corporation Court. He expected to get another incorrigible boy, Willie Spence, but while waiting Justice Taylor had an application from that boy's aunt and allowed her to take the boy to train.

Smith says there are 119 pupils at the school, or nineteen more than the State provides for, but he is not willing to refuse any children who can be benefited by the training. He was formerly a minister to Liberia, and speaks interestingly of that country for the benefit of thrifty colored people. But he is better satisfied to work where he was born—in Virginia. There are 225 acres of corn under cultivation by the boys of the school and thirty-five acres of cucumbers. On the latter crop there was an income of $570 last year.

Lizzie E. Mabry lost her case in the United States Court by the decision of Judge Waddill this morning. She brought a suit for $10,000 as the administratrix of her husband and for ...e loss of his life by drowning. He was keeper on the Norfolk and Western Railway bridge, and was knocked off the bridge and drowned by the collision of the tug Helen, in passing the draw of the Southern Branch.

The question was on the nature of the case. The defense demurred that the case was not in admiralty, because the accident did not happen on the water, but to the bridge on the land. Judge Waddill agreed that the case was not one of libel. There is a similar suit pending in the civil court.

Miss Young, of Raleigh, N. C., who is a guest at one of the Virginia Beach cottages, had a miraculous escape from drowning while bathing at the Beach last evening. Miss Young and her escort, a young gentlman from Petersburg, were carried by the current beyond their depth and the escort found himself unable to assist Miss Young. Messrs. Whitehurst and Fantone seeing the situation rushed at once to the drowning lady's assistance and brought her from the water unconscious. Miss Young had not fully recovered last night, and was to-day still suffering from her experience.

DIED WHILE ABROAD.

Information has been received here of the death, while traveling in Europe, of Mr. Samuel A. Stevens, formerly a prominent citizen of Norfolk. At the time of his demise he was a resident of Leominster, Mass., in which place he held the position of member of the Water Board and president of the Board of Trade. He was traveling abroad with friends.

The funeral of Dr. Edwin G. Hank, of the Tanner's Creek section of Norfolk county, who was killed by his horse last Saturday night, took place this morning at 10 o'clock from the Denby's Methodist Church, in the county, and was largely attended.

In swinging around in the stream at the navy yard, the United States monitor Arkansas collided with the bow of the receiving ship Richmond. No damage was sustained by the receiving ship, although the force of the blow caused her to drag her anchors, making it necessary to reset them. The monitor sustained probably $400 damage, two boats being wrecked by the collision.

NORFOLK, VA., August 4.—Frank Clark, of Baltimore, about thirty years of age, was arrested this afternoon upon the charge of taking from her mother for immoral purposes Theresa Murray, the sixteen-year-old daughter of Mrs. Mary E. Murray, of No. 340 Chapel Street.

Naval Board of Inspection is here from Washington to-day. Captain Francis J. Train, chairman, did not come, but Captains Cowles, Roper and Woodard made an inspection of the Nevada, now at the yard. The ship pased a satisfactory inspection says as to her turrets and the board is confident that the alterations to the rollers now being made here will be successful.

Two judges appointed by the fusion faction of the Democratic party in the party, have refused to serve on the primary election to occur on Thursday. George Washington Griggs, the mulatto recently convicted of a criminal assault on Marion, the four-year-old daughter of Mr. Bruce Mason, of Port Norfolk, was sentenced to-day by Judge Portlock in Portsmouth. For eighteen years in the penitentiary. It was a particularly vicious assault, and there was a threat of lynching, but the officers protected the negro.

Lancaster Williams, of Richmond. In the Samuel White case there was a hung jury. The fireman of the York Street engine house sued the Norfolk Railway and Light Company, for $7,500 for personal injuries. In a collision between the fire engine and a stret car last winter. White was thrown from the engine and suffered a broken nose and bruises. The case was on trial two days and the jury considered it from noon yesterday till this morning without agreeing. The jury was dismissed as unable to make a verdict.

COAL SALES NOT BRISK.

The price of hard coal was increased to the dealers ten cents a ton at the mines on the first of the month. But the price has not changed here. It sells here for $7 a ton, but not briskly. There is a small supply of hard coal, and there are not many schooners arriving. The advices from northern cities are that the supply is not great and all of the June orders from here were not filled in July. There is no sale of soft coal for domestic use, so that practically all of the soft coal in the market now is the steam coal, which for the run of the mine grade sells for $8.25 a ton. That coal is here in abundance. It is selling freely, but one dealer says he could take 10,000 tons and not be overstocked.

ORDER TO MOVE FROM WEST SIDE

Colored Man Received Anonymous Letter.

TEN DAYS IS THE LIMIT

Is Only Negro Family Living West of River.
TEN DAYS IS THE LIMIT
M. E. McKelley, a colored man employed by the street railway company living at 914 West Douglas avenue, the only colored man living west of the river, received an anonymous letter ordering him to move from the West Side within ten days. The letter is as follows:

West Wichita
Aug 23, 1903.

Mr. McKelly
Sir—

I write you this as a notice that the best thing for you to do is move from this side of the river you are the only black family on this side and we dont allow such people here so the sooner you move the better for you now take warning at this for you wont be given over ten days to get out.

West End mob
grasshopper Ike in Command.

The letter was written on cheap note paper with a lead pencil. The writing is very poor, no punctuation was used and few capitals. The above is verbatim.

Mr. McKelley has been living on the West Side since last spring. For years there has been but one colored family living on the West Side and this is the first time that any one has sent a letter to them ordering them to move away. Mr. McKelley lived here twelve of fifteen years ago and worked for the Crystal ice plant several years and was there at the time of the explosion of a tank in the building. He worked at the Wichita steam laundry for a couple of years and then went to Nebraska.

Many West Side people were shown the letter yesterday and it occasioned considerable surprise among the business men and residents, as none had ever thought of ordering Mr. McKelley and his family to move from that side of the river and it was on the advice of the business men that Mr. McKelley decided that he would not move from his present home at the present time.

Mr. McKelley was pretty well scared when he received the letter but those who read it have tried to treat the matter as a joke but the colored man and his wife do not feel that it was written in fun. The letter was shown to the police and detectives are trying to locate the man who wrote the letter.

HAGERSTOWN.—The Pennsylvania Railroad has begun to widen its trackway through this county. The work of excavating at Jackson's Hill is already under way. The hill became famous when the United States government built the National road, for it was here that the government engineers were utterly unable to proceed with the work of excavating on account of the tremendous flow of water from springs they encountered in the hill. The government stopped all work on the National road and for years the place was literally covered with broken wagons, carts, scoops, harness and hundreds of tons of stone hauled from the Elkhorn quarries, ten miles distant.

BRAZIL.—Miss Mamie Goodhue, on returning from a party to her home in Knightsville, Friday night, found a burly negro trying to break into her room. She gave the alarm and a posse quickly gathered. Reed for the meeting here of the Young People's Union of the Colored Baptist churches of the State, to be held at the Second Baptist Church on July 21-22. Two brothers, Lanta and Smiley Pauley, committed suicide some months ago and the supposition is that Barton, the third brother, has killed himself.

Worrill, in New Albany, and selling it to Decker for 60 cents. Mr. Decker denies the charge.

The assets are $1,000 and the liabilities are $1,700. * * * The Fowler sawmill here has been sold to Bruce Calvert, and Frank Fowler will embark in the lumber business in Kentucky.

HYMERA.—At the township commencement exercises Friday evening twenty-nine pupils received diplomas of graduation from the public schools. The class is the largest ever graduated from this township and larger than any other class in the county at least in recent years. Dr. A. J. Kinnaman, of the Central Normal College at Danville, delivered the address.

ROCKVILLE.—Rockville is experiencing one of the most substantial building booms in its history. There are now at least ten new modern residences contemplated, costing from $3,000 to $10,000, while severel other houses are contemplated. Carpenters and contractors have all the work they can do and there is a marked scarcity of workmen.

LAPEL.—William Reynolds, who had been swimming with a crowd of men and boys west of town, tried to board an east-bound train at 5:30 o'clock Saturday afternoon to come home. He slipped and fell and lost his right leg. He is twenty-five years old and has a wife and one child.

RICHMOND.—The second annual session of the First and Second districts of the South Ohio conference of the Wesleyan Methodist Sunday-schools will convene in this city July 24.

MOB IS CHEATED OF ITS VICTIM Assailant of Miss Olson Taken to Glencoe to Prevent Lynching-He Confesses.
MONTEVIDEO, Minn., July 19.—The negro assailant of Miss Helen Oson, who was captured near Milan, was taken through to Glencoe on a special train, to avoid the lynching which would have been a certainty if he had been brought here.

There was a crowd of several hundred at the depot here when the train passed through, but the sight of several deputies heavily armed prevented an attack on the train.

NEGRO FIEND NARROWLY ES-
CAPES LYNCHING AT
MONTEVIDEO.

COMMITTED MURDEROUS ASSAULT

PRISONER LODGED IN GLENCOE
JAIL—FRANKLY CONFESSES
HIS GUILT.
OFFICERS HOLD MOB AT BAY
CAPTURED BY POSSE AFTER BEING WOUNDED DURING HARD CHASE.
Scott, the negro who so brutally assaulted Miss Helen Olson Saturday morning at Watson, was, was safely lodged in jail here at 5 o'clock yesterday morning.

The negro makes no hesitancy in admitting his guilt.

The crime occurred between 4 and 5 o'clock Saturday morning. Miss Olson, who is a milliner twenty-three years old, and a friend, Miss Julia Torgenson, were alone in the house, Miss Olson's father being in Minneapolis under a doctor's care.

The young women were awakened by a man whom Miss Torgenson said she thought was a negro. The fellow demanded money and jewels. Miss Olson said she would give him all the money in the house if he would promise to leave at once. He replied: "You get the money!"

Hit Her With an Axe.

The fellow seized Miss Olson, dragged her from bed and down the stairs. She fought and screamed, and the man struck her a terrific blow on the forehead with an axe and she fell to the floor unconscious.

Miss Torgenson climbed out of the bed room window onto a porch and screamed for help, when a man rushed from the house, and after niring a shot from a revolver at Miss Torgenson, disappeared in the darkness.

The screams and the shot aroused the neighbors, who rushed to the scene. Miss Olson was found unconscious, lying in a pool of blood. The entire town was aroused and posses were formed to search for the murderer. Posses also started out from Montevideo.

Captured by a Posse.

The negro was seen Saturday afternoon by one of the posses, and he was chased several miles before he was caught. During the pursuit he was shot in the left arm with a rifle.

Chief of Police Denny of Ortonville and several deputies took charge of him and carried him to Marlan, a small station on the Milwaukee road. At 3 o'clock Sunday morning an excursion train from Milbank pulled into the station, the wounded man was placed in an empty coach and both of the doors were guarded by men with rifles.

When the train reached Montevideo word had been received of the capture, and several hundred infuriated men stood on the platform, armed with rifles, revolvers and shotguns, and carrying ropes, clamoring for the negro's life.

Mob Seeks His Life.

When his whereabouts were at last discovered a rush was made for the car, but the mob was met by rifles, and Chief Denny threatened to shoot the first man who boarded the steps. Armed men attempted to mount the train, but only those who had excursion tickets were admitted, and the train was finally pulled out safely.

At this juncture, Chief Denny declares, the mob, had it been led by a determined man, could with but little trouble have overpowered them and captured the negro.

When the train arrived at Glencoe the prisoner was hurried into a carriage and driven to the county jail, where he was locked up before any of the citizens knew of his arrival.

His Victim Will Die.

Montevideo, Minn., July 20. — Miss Helena Olson of Watson, who was murderously assaulted by the negro Scott, is still alive, but there are no hopes of recovery. The excitement is dying out and it is thought that there will be no further attempt at lynching.

MONTEVIDEO WAS NOT IN HANDS OF A MOB
Negroes Driven Out of Town by Schoolmates of Miss Olson.
Special to The Globe. MONTEVIDEO. Minn.
Special to The Globe.

MONTEVIDEO, Minn., July 22.—The false statements published concerning Montevideo people, claiming they were organized into a terrible mob to lynch the negro who assaulted and, as he supposed, murdered Helen Olson, of Watson, in justice to this city should be contradicted. The fire bell was rung Saturday morning at 9 o'clock. Sheriff Chas. Hartley called in the name of the state for all citizens to aid him in capturing the negro. All able bodied, courageous men obeyed at once, armed themselves with shot guns and rifles and commenced the search. These men were organized and stationed at all points on the various roads and alleys to make sure that the negro did not escape in the night. Many of them remained at their posts until Sunday morning and did not know that the negro had been caught at Milan or that he was on any train, consequently the crowd that was at, the depot was merely a lot of curious boys and possibly a few crippled old men. This crowd is described in the daily papers as "a terrible mob at Montevideo." It is true that Sheriff Hartley and his friends did not want to take the chances of bringing the negro to the county jail, as it was possible that when the several hundred negro hunters should get back to town a mob might have been organized, especially after the negro had made a full confession.

As to the mob driving the negroes out of Montevideo, this movement was all arranged and carried out by young boys who were classmates and personal friends of Helen Olson. They threatened no violence, simply asked the few negroes to leave the city and they did. A crowd of school boys anywhere might act the same—under similar circumstances.

AFTER A LIVELY CHASE.
Minnesota Officers Save Negro From Being Strung Up.
Glencoe, Minn., July 24.—A thousand angry and excited men and boys made a second attempt to lynch Joseph Scott, the negro who murderously assaulted Minnie Olson at Watson.

Sheriffs Hartley and McKenzie attempted to take the negro from Glencoe to the Montevideo jail and succeeded in getting him as far as Minnesota Falls, when the mob caught up.

Here the mob demanded the prisoner and the sheriffs, realizing that to remain on the train was useless, drew their revolvers and made a dash for a livery stable. The howling mass of humanity followed into the stable and while the horses were being hitched for the flight of the sheriffs with their prisoner a hand-to-hand fight ensued.

montevedio-montevedio-1903-08.A22:
The Insanity Dodge.
One of the colored attorneys of Minneapolis refers to the negro Scott, who made a murderous assault upon Helen Olson at Watson, as a person of unsound mind and is particular to call attention to the fellow's recent release from an insane hospital in South Dakota. A few days ago The Free Press made the statement that Scott himself was laying the foundation for a defense by declaring that he had been an inmate of an insane hospital. No doubt an effort will be made by his lawyer to secure his release on that ground, but jurors will exhibit sound sense by paying no attention to such a defense. Scott's mind on the night the assault was committed was working well. He coolly planned the attack and he has since stated in a published interview that his motive was robbery; that he overheard Miss Olson tell someone in the house that she had a sum of money there. He made up his mind to have the money. On entering the house he carried an axe with him so that he could use it in case it became necessary to subdue the occupants. Scott was not insane when he prepared and put into execution his plans, and it is not thought that any sensible person will be hoodwinked into believing that he was. This insanity dodge is worked to the limit by criminals, and the latter are encouraged to do so altogether too much by attorneys who are more than anxious to have their clients acquitted of serious charges. Is it any wonder that people rise up and take the law into their own hands when such a condition of things confronts them?

montevedio-montevedio-1903-08.A28:
CONVICTED NEGRO MAKES CONFESSION
He Tells of Robbery at Watson, Minn., and Felonious Assault Upon Olson Girl.
Happy in the knowledge that he was at last safe from a threatening mob, Joe Scott, the negro who attempted to kill Helen Olson at Watson, Minn., last July, sat in a cell at the county jail last night and related in detail the story of his crime, the first complete confession the negro has made since his capture on the day following the attempted murder.

Scott told how he had landed at the little village of Watson in a box car, which had been sidetracked there, of how he later heard people talking about money while passing the home of Helen Olson, and how he waited until the lights in the house had been extinguished, when he removed a screen and entered the house for the purpose of robbery.

Scott was to have had his trial at Montevideo this week, but when arraigned in court Tuesday afternoon he weakened and pleaded guilty to the charges against him, being immediately sentenced to thirty years in the penitentiary.

Fearing that the mob, which filled the court house and crowded the streets of the town, might attempt to lynch the negro, Sheriff Hartley, assisted by several deputies, brought the negro to St. Paul on the first train which left Montevideo following the disposal of Scott's case.

Even with this precaution a threatening mob followed the party to the train, and Scott felt much easier when he was well out of the mob's sight. Today he will be taken to Stillwater to serve his sentence of thirty years.

Makes Public Confession.

While in the county jail last night Scott sent for a Globe reporter, stating that he desired before going to prison to give a correct account of the crime and the incidents which led up to it. He made no attempt whatever to shield himself, except to reiterate that the crime was not premeditated, but the result of a temporary aberration of the mind.

Scott's statement to The Globe was as follows:

"I've got my sentence now and I want to tell the truth of this case. To begin with, I had just been released from the North Dakota penitentiary, and was beating my way through the country in a box car. I went to sleep and when I awoke I found that the car I was in had been side tracked. I got out and walked over to the stock yards to get a drink of water, and in walking around I passed the Olson house. A number of people were standing in the yard and I heard them say something about money. I needed money, so I decided I would rob the house that night. I kept out of sight until quite late, when I got into the house through a window.

Went Three Times to the House.

"I searched everywhere for money, but I could not find any, so I went up stairs, and finally went into a bed room where two girls were sleeping. One was the Olson girl and the other was a girl named, as I have later learned, Julia Torgenson. When they awoke I demanded money, but they said there was not any in the house. I parleyed with them and finally left. I went back the second time, and after another unsuccessful attempt, I left again. Then for the third time I went back. This time the Olson girl said there was a little money down stairs and she went down with me to get it. The other girl did not come down, and I guess they were both scared, for the last time I went in I took an ax which I had found in the yard. After the girl had given me the money, about $2, I struck her in the head with an ax, after which I called to the girl up stairs to come down, as I had hurt the Olson girl. I then got out of the house and tried to make my escape. I walked all night and the next day I slept in the woods.

"Along in the evening I woke up and saw people riding along the road with guns and rifles. I knew they were looking for me, and when I attempted to get away they saw me, and I started to run. DESPERATE NEGRO WOUNDS THREE MEN.
Shot by Patrolman Miller While Resisting Arrest. After making a fierce attack on two
After making a fierce attack on two patrolmen and a citizen, each of whom he seriously cut on the head with an improvised weapon of iron, Raphael Harvey, a desperate negro, was twice shot early this morning, and then beaten into submission. He is now at the police station house.

The negro was found in Perry lane near Jefferson, and Officer Mose Davis in plain clothes, attempted to arrest him on suspicion of having held up and robbed a lady. He attacked Davis and Patrolman Enoch Hartley, who went to Davis' assistance. Frank Goolsby, a Central Railway engineer, attracted to the scene of the difficulty went to the help of the officers and was in turn badly wounded by the desperate negro.

Harvey was armed with a piece of iron some two feet long, three inches wide and just thick enough to make it a weapon of the most dangerous character, when wielded by a powerful and desperate man. With this weapon he inflicted a severe wound on the head of each of the men who attempted the arrest, wounds of so serious a nature that after they had been dressed by Dr. G. W. Herlot, to whose office the wounded men were carried, it was found necessary to send them to the Savannah Hospital.

Officer Hartley is the worst hurt. He received a gash on the head some four or five inches long, and in addition a second gash on the right arm. Davis received a cut on his forehead, just at the edge of the hair. Goolsby, the man who went to the assistance of the officers, was badly cut on the head.

The negro then fled, but about twenty minutes later was located in an outhouse in Liberty lane, near Tattnall street, where he was surrounded by the police. When Officer Harmon Miller entered the place to make the arrest the negro started for him, and the officer was forced to shoot. He fired twice, striking the man once in the arm and again in the body, although wounded Harvey continued vicious. He offered such resistance that it was necessary to use a stick on him before he was sufficiently subdued to be taken to the station house.

The negro has been identified as the same man with whom Officer Mose Davis had a desperate encounter in Oglethorpe lane near Bull street some four months ago. At that time he attacked the patrolman when he attempted to arrest him, used him up pretty badly and escaped.
rafe-harvey-savannah-1903-02-15.A2:
FOUGHT IN THE DARK
HOW DESPERATE NEGRO DID UP OFFICERS AND CITIZEN.
IS DANGEROUSLY WOUNDED.
MARVEY IN JAIL HOSPITAL SUF- FERING FROM DOZEN WOUNDS.
Patrolman Hartley and Seaboard
Air Line Engineer Goolsby at the Savannah Hospital Badly Wounded as a Result of Their Encounter With Vicious Negro-Officer Davis Not So Badly Hurt-Unarmed, Hartley Was in a Dark Room With Harvey Alone—Police Had Trouble Protecting Prisoner.

As a result of their encounter in a house in Perry lane, near Montgomery street, with a desperate negro early yesterday morning, an account of which was given in the Morning News, Patrolman Hartley and John Goolsby, a Seaboard Air Line engineer, are at the Savannah Hospital.

Although not considered dangerously wounded, both men are suffering a great deal of pain and are not permitted to see any one. Officer Mose Davis, who at the same time received an ugly gash in the head, is not so badly hurt, and is at his home. Reaf Harvey, the negro who caused all of the trouble, is in the hospital at the county jail, and his condition is regarded as dangerous. He is suffering from two pistol shot wounds, inflicted by Patrolman Miller, and several scalp wounds, inflicted by other officers.

At large flatiron and a heavy iron bar, the weapons used by the negro in his attack upon the officers and Goolsby, are held at police headquarters as evidence, and if Harvey recovers he will have to answer three charges of assault with intent to murder. That the negro was not killed when first tackled in Perry lane was due to the fact that the fight in which he was victorious was made in the dark, and the officers were afraid to shoot for fear that they would wound each other. This was made clear by Officer Davis yesterday, when he made a full statement of the affray to the superintendent of police.

Arrested as Suspect.

Davis had been engaged with Detective Murphy in a search for the negro, who robbed Miss McLeod, but no trace of him had been found. The officers separated, and a few minutes later Davis saw a negro on Perry lane and Jefferson street. The man was acting suspiciously, and the officer in plain clothes placed him under arrest. At that time Davis did not recognize the negro as the one who had done him up and escaped under fire several months before in Oglethorpe lane, near the Independent Presbyterian Church.

At the corner of Perry lane, and Montgomery street Harvey pulled away from the officer, and for the first time Davis recognized him. The negro is fleet-footed, and when he turned and ran, Davis fired one shot at him. Harvey secured himself in a house and barricaded the door, and windows. Patrolman Hartley and one or two belated citizens, including the Seaboard Air Line engineer, were attracted by the trouble and went to the assistance of Davis. A boy with a bicycle agreed to let the men have his lamp and make a search of the premises.

Fought in the Dark.

No sooner, however, had the lamp been pushed inside the door that a blow from the negro sent it to the floor and extinguished it. This left the room in darkness and the burly and vicious negro had things practically his own way. He struck Davis a blow across the head that sent him staggering backward into the laned, and a second blow sent Engineer Goolsby in the same direction.

About the same time the door to the room was closed and Hartley was left in the room with the desperate negro. The officer had loaned his pistol to a citizen who was assisting and only had his club. He was at the mercy of the negro and blow after blow fell upon his head. The heavy iron bar made deep gashes in the scalp and Hartley fell to the floor unconscious.

Jumped Back Fence.

Harvey made his escape by jumping over the back fence and had disappeared when Patrolman Miller answered the distress whistles. Hartley and Goolsby were both unable to continue in the search and were taken at once to the office of Dr. Heriot, from where the were sent to the hospital.

Although the wound in his head bled profusely Davis continued in the search for the negro and piloted his brother officers through the neighboring lanes. Several officers had been hurried to the scene and the search continued. The camping grounds of Harvey, well known to the police, were gone over carefully and outbuildings in Liberty lane were being searched, when Patrolman Miller located the negro in an outbuilding near Barnard street.

Fought, Although Wounded.

As the officer struck a match Harvey sprang for him. In a moment the man in uniform had fired two bullets into the negro, who seized his arms and grappled with him. Harvey is a powerful individual, and he had a strong grip on Miller. Mounted Sergeant Wood was only a few feet away and with others jumped for the negro.

Several hard blows from the clubs of the officers landed on the prisoner's head, making a dozen wounds that sent blood over the officers. It was with difficulty that the police prevented citizens who had gathered from finishing the negro, who continued insolent, although badly wounded. Even though Harvey recovers he has a long term in the pentitentiary ahead of him.

The negro is well know in police circles and has a hard name. He has been in trouble with the officers upon innumerable occasions and would have been killed by Detective Murphy three or four years ago had not a woman jumped in front of the officer and prevented his firing. Upon that occasion Harvey hurled a brick at the officer's head. After his fight several months ago with Officer Davis, he kept out of the way although the police were looking for him.

The wounded engineer is not Mr. Frank Goolsby, employed by the Central of Georgia Railway Company. Mr. Frank Goolsby was on the road at the time of the trouble and was kept busy explaining yesterday that he had not been hurt.
rafe-harvey-savannah-1903-02-15.A3:
HARVEY DIED IN JAIL
NEGRO DESPERADO, MORTALLY WOUNDED, ENDED LIFE IN PRISON.
SHOT BY OFFICER MILLER.
HAD BADLY BEATEN THREE MEN BEFORE HE WAS ARRESTED.
Notorious and Vicious Negro Laid Out Patrolmen Mose Davis and Hartley, and Seaboard Air Line Engineer Goolsby, Before He Was Located and Shot in Stable in Liberty Lane Two Weeks Ago. Shot Twice by Miller and Beaten by Officers and Citizens.

After suffering two weeks from pistol shot wounds inflicted by Patrolman Harmon Miller, whom he attempted to kill, after having knocked out Patrolmen Enoch Hartley and Mose Davis, and Seaboard Air Line Engineer John Goolsby, Rafe Harvey, a notorious negro, died in the jail hospital last night.

Besides being shot, Harvey was badly beaten by officers and citizens before he was made a prisoner, and it was believed from the first that he would die. The negro made vicious assaults upon three men before he was located by Patrolman Miller in a stable in Liberty lane, near Barnard street. When run to cover in the stable he made a desperate effort to brain Patrolman Miller, and was shot twice while advancing upon the man in uniform.

Early on the morning of Feb. 15, while looking for a negro, who had held up and robbed a Miss McLeod, Officer Mose Davis ran into Harvey in Perry lane, near Montgomery street. The negro was acting in a suspicious manner, and was made a prisoner by the man in plain clothes. But before Davis had moved a foot with his man Harvey let fly a right under the eye that staggered and dazed the officer. When Davis recovered Harvey was fifty yards away and making for a house. The patrolman fired one shot, but was unable to stop the negro, who barricaded himself in the house.

Barricaded in a House.

Not until he was assaulted did the patrolman recognize Harvey as a negro who had gotten the best of him in a hard fight in Oglethorpe lane, near Bull street, during the summer, when the mysterious burglar was at work. At that time Harvey had shown that he was a desperate character and Davis realized that he would have to have assistance. He blew his whistle for aid and the call was answered by Patrolman Hartley. Engineer Goolsby and a white boy also put in an appearance and plans were laid to break into the house in which Harvey had locked himself.

The boy furnished the officers and engineer with a bicycle lamp, but as it was pushed into the room Harvey smashed it with an iron bar. Protected by darkness he used this bar and a smoothing iron and sent first Davis, and then Goolsby, staggering through the door with ugly wounds in their heads. Hartley was beaten into insensibility and fell upon the floor in the room. Harvey then escaped through the rear and got away by jumping over a fence. In the meantime the fact that two officers and a citizen had been done up by a negro was made known at police headquarters and a squad of men, with Mounted Sergeant Woods, was put on the trail of the negro.

Desperado in a Stable.

A systematic search was made, and about an hour later, after the assault was committed, Harvey was found by Patrolman Miller in the stable in Liberty lane, within fifty yards of the home of the superintendent of police. As soon as the uniformed man found his way into the stable Harvey made for him, and he found it necessary to use his revolver. One bullet entered the negro's shoulder and the other lodged in the abdomen. Although fatally wounded, the negro closed in on the officer and had to be beaten with clubs and billies in the hands of other officers and citizens. He was finally subdued, but was suffering from a dozen wounds when landed at the police station house.

Harvey was known to the police as a vicious negro, and was a fugitive from justice for several months before he was shot. He gave the police no end of trouble, and was considered a desperate character. The negro would have been shot about four years ago by Detective Murphy, at that time a uniformed man, but for the fact that a woman jumped in front of the officer and prevented his firing. The negro had encounters with quite a number of officers at various times and was credited with being able to outrun any man in the department.

In this connection I desire to suggest to the merchants of Savannah that when they close their places of business at night it would be wise for them to leave lights burning, and their window curtains up, so that the interior of their places can be seen without trouble from the street. I am convinced that one of my men passed the Foye & Eckstein store and tried the front door while the safe blowers were at work. It was impossible, however, for this safe to have been seen from the street.

When I took charge of the department I found that the men on fire detail at night were required to answer all alarms. It often happened that they were gotten out of their beds in all sorts of weather, to learn that a chimney had burned out, or that some trivial blaze had been extinguished before the alarm had ceased sounding.

In order to lighten the duties of the men on fire detail I issued instructions to the men on the streets to report by telephone at once to the desk sergeant the nature of any fires in their precincts. RAGE TROUBLE WAS SERIOUSLY EXPECTED.
VAUGHANVILLE WAS THROWN INTO GREAT EXCITEMENT FRIDAY NIGHT.
Negro Odd Fellows Hall Was Burned--Assistance From Newberry Was Asked and Rendered.
Serious race trouble was threatened at Vaughanville, in the upper portion of the county, near the Laurens line, on Friday night. The trouble, however, seems to have passed over without other serious result than the burning of the negro Odd Fellow's hall, the members of which organization were supposed to be at the bottom of the trouble which was expected.

On Friday afternoon the report became circulated at Vaughanville that the negroes had sent to Chappells for arms, and that they would hold a meeting at the Odd Fellows' hall Friday night, after which they would wait on young Clareuce M. Brooks, who on Saturday night a week ago shot and killed a negro, Raymond Sizer, as the coroner's jury said, in self-defense, and that they would also call upon the gentlemen who helped to bury Sizer. The account of this shooting, together with the evidence taken at the coroner's inquest, was published in The Herald and News at the time. Sizer was a prominent member of the negro lodge of Odd Fellows, which has long been a disturbing element in the community. It will be remembered that after the inquest Sizer's relatives or any other negroes refused to touch the body, and that a coffin was made and the body buried by the white people, the members of the coroner's jury and young Brooks' attorney, Mr. Cole. L. Blease, assisting in the interment. The relatives of the dead negro had ordered a coffin from Cross Hill, but turned it back when it reached Vaughanville. Next day after the body was buried by the white people the negroes opened the grave, placed the body in another coffin, and reburied it at a point about a mile distant from the first grave. The reason for this action and why the negroes should wish to call upon the white men who buried the body, is unexplained.

Since Sizer's death the negro Odd Fellows, of which he was a member, have held very frequent meetings, a representative of The Herald and News was informed by the people of Vaughanville, and have made numerous threats. These threats, taken in connection with the reports which became circulated Friday afternoon, caused great excitement in the community, and serious trouble was feared.

A 'phone message was sent to Newberry for assistance at about four o'clock Friday afternoon, and a party of twelve immediately left for Vaughanville, twenty-one miles distant. When the Newberry party, accompanied by a representative of The Herald and News, arrived on the scene, there was no indication of trouble, except there were about thirty five white men in the little store of Mr. Whit Goodwyn, armed to the teeth with double-barrelled shot guns and small arms, and prepared to meet any trouble which might occur. The addition of the Newberry party made about fifty.
vaughanville-vaughanville-1903-10-16.A4:
A meeting was called to order by Mr. Cole L. Blease and the situation was discussed. A detachment of twelve men was sent to the Odd Fellows' hall at about 9 o'clock to see if the expected meeting of negroes would be held. There was no light in the building and no one was found.

Shortly after the prrty returned to the store, the building, a loosely constructed, two-story frame structure, was seen to be ablaze, and it soon burned to the ground. The conflagration lighted up the country for miles around. The building was the property of the negro Odd Fellows and was not of any great value. The first floor was used for a negro school. It was situated about a quarter of a mile from Mr. Goodwyn's store and was near an old negro church. The fire occurred some time before 11 o'clock. How it started is not known.

The situation was again discussed. It was proposed to visit the negroes who are supposed to be the ringleaders and to give them correction, but this motion was immediately opposed by Mr. Fred H. Dominick, who was seconded by Mr. Blease and the officers of the law, Deputy Sheriff Duncan Johnson and Constable C. G. Blease, and the proposal was almost unanimously voted down, the gentlemen present saying emphatically they had come to protect the white people of the community and young Brooks, and not to create a disturbance.

It was feared that trouble might result later in the night, and it was decided that the men should sleep under arms, and sentinels were posted. A number slept in the store and the others in the surrounding homes.

The representative of The Herald and News called upon young Brooks' father. Mr. Brooks said he was convinced that, had not prompt action been taken and assistance received, the negroes would have attempted hurt to his family, and especially his son, during the night.

Nothing unusual developed during the night and next morning most of the party returned to their homes, several remaining in case any further trouble occurred.

The negro Odd Fellows, whose hall was burned, The Herald and News man was informed by the people of Vaughanville, has exercised a baneful influence over the negroes of the community since their organization several years ago. The names of Isaac Fortune, Jones Pitts, West Bates, Jim Wade and Ben Watts were given as the ringleaders. It is said the hall has been used as a general assembly hall for the negroes, where they met under the mantle of secrecy and hatched their schemes without fear of interruption. When a representative of The Herald and News passed by the site of the hall on his return home Saturday morning, the embers were still smouldering. Posted around on the trees were notices, signed by officers of the lodge, warning all against smoking on the premises. This is the third race trouble threatened at Vaughanville in recent years. Several years ago it
