uprising and there was a great deal of excitement for a time, with the result that the doctor was run out of the community. A year later the same experience was repeated with another negro doctor, J. W. T. Patterson, with the same result.

Clarence Brooks, the young man who killed the negro Sizer, and whose act was the cause of the threatened negro uprising, is the seventeen-year-old son of Mr. C. A. Brooks. He is under $200 bond and it is said will be prosecuted.

It is a matter of congratulation to the people of the community and the whole county, that the affair on Friday night ended with so little serious results. Had there been any demonstration by the negroes there is no doubt that blood would have been freely spilt. All is quiet for the present, but it is not know at what time the trouble will break out again.

NEGRO REPORTED KILLED.

It has been reported on the streets of Newberry and elsewhere throughout the county that early Friday night a negro, carrying a lighted lantern, was seen near the Odd Fellows' hall, and that when he was questioned and replied that he was a black man, he was fired upon and killed. A representative of The Herald and News reached the scene shortly after 8 o'clock Friday night and remained until 7 o'clock Saturday morning, and no such act came within his notice. It may be that some one was fired upon, but it appears that the report that any one was killed is unfounded.

AN ORDERLY CROWD.

The party that went up to Vaughanville from Newberry went to protect the people of Vaughanville if it should be necessary and not to create a disturbance, and the Newberry party kept strictly within the purpose for which it went.

Special Judge Tom Crice yesterday afternoon late assessed a fine of $15 and costs against "Rev." W. M. Grayor, the colored preacher charged with using incendiary language on the streets and inciting the ignorant classes who hear him to commit acts tending to create trouble. He paid his fine and costs, amounting to about $30, and is still in he city so far as is known.

It seems there is no objection to free speech, but some of the language used by Grayor is said to have a tendency to incite race trouble, and as he has been warned to desist and hasn't done it, there is a disposition in some quarters to make him "move on." Marshal Crow thinks a great many dogs have no legal right to reside in Paducah because no license has been paid on them. Sunday Shooting at Clayton.
On Sunday afternoon, the 13th instant, at Carpenter Bros. camps near Bethel church, Frank LeSuer was fatally wounded by a negro, who was familiarly known about the camps as Booze Bennette. The difficulty arose over a dispute the negro had with another white man employed by the construction company and which Mr. LaSuer was called upon to settle. The wound inflicted on Mr. LaSuer was made with a breach-loading, single barrel gun, with an ounce of No. 6 shot and was fired at very short range. An ugly wound measuring some three inches in diameter was made a little below the center of the abdomen.

Physicians were summoned and did all they could for the sufferer, keeping him alive until 6 o'clock Monday morning, when he died.

Mr. LaSuer hailed originally from New York, but had been South some time. His remains were buried at Bethel on Tuesday morning. The murderer was captured on the high trestle in Tallulah Falls about sunset Sunday, just as he was about to board the down train, and was lodged in jail here Monday night.—Clayton (Ga.) Tribune, December 17.

A mission of the Christian Catholic church, John Alexander Dowie, overseer, was established at Chattanooga, Tenn., last Saturday. It starts with forty members. William D. Gay has been placed in charge and will hold regular services.

The body of Frank A. LeSeur, who was murdered by Booze Bennett several weeks ago at Clayton, Ga., was exhumed last week and shipped to Boliver, N. Y. It is stated that an Atlanta woman, to whom LeSeur was engaged, ordered the body taken up and shipped to Boliver, and that she bore all expenses.

Six persons were killed and fourteen injured as the result of an explosion of gas in the cafe of a hotel in Bognonas, France, last Friday. The hotel was partially wrecked. From stories of the survivors of the explosion it was learned that a dozen patrons of the hotel were sitting at the tables drinking and playing cards when an odor of gas penetrated the room.

Harry D. Egbert, who murdered John G. Saxton and John West last October, was hanged at Salem, Oregon, last Friday. Egbert made a brief speech on the scaffold. He said: "My friends, take me as a mark; keep your children off the street and above all, out of the saloons. Bad raising and bad company are the direct cause of my downfall. I have repented my sins."

Elberton, Ga., suffered severely from a destructive fire last Wednesday night. The Jones block, in which were a drug store, two general stores and a photograph gallery, were burned, with practically their entire contents. The loss was about $12,000 in excess of insurance. Merchants in nearby stores lost considerable sums by moving goods and getting them damaged. Elberton has no fire department and the flames were fought by bucket brigades.

Mrs. Mary Schrofrenski, aged 125, the oldest person in the country, according to the age given in the death certificate, died last Saturday at the home of her daughter, at Menominee, Mich. She was born in Prussia and came to this country twenty-two years ago. Her father lived to be 100 years old, and her youngest daughter, Mrs. Mary Lowendski, is nearly seventy years old. The children are so poor that the body was buried by the county.

Bass Bracewell died at his home near Dexter, Ga., on January 29, after a lingering illness. Bracewell was dangerously ill, but being a believer in faith cure he refused, it is stated, to have any medical attention, and was carried from house to house to the different faith cure meetings. He was at one of these meetings endeavoring to stand and sing when death seized him. His first wife died last year under similar circumstances. She would not receive any medical aid until it was too late. Bracewell is the son of J. R. Bracewell, also a firm believer in the same faith. He leaves a second wife, who was a sister of his former wife.

wm-johnston-new-york-1903-07-12.A1:
NEGROES BESET POLICE
USE PISTOLS AND BRICKS.
Rioters Flee to Roofs-Pedestrian Fires with Patrolman.
A riot, suppressed by the reserves of three police stations, broke out last night among negroes in the tenement houses in West Sixty-second-st., between West End and Amsterdam aves., about 6 o'clock.

A crowd of negroes was standing next door to a saloon at No. 236 West Sixty-second-st. As Policeman Connor was about to pass them, some of the negroes began to threaten him, and acted in such a disorderly manner that he ordered them to move.

"We'll stay here as long as we please," shouted one of the gang, William Johnson, according to Connor, advancing on the policeman.

Connor pushed the negro back, but the latter sprang at him and struck him on the neck. The policeman drew his club and seized the negro's jersey. Seeing that their comrade could not get away, the gang swarmed about the policeman and followed him across the street, muttering threateningly.

When in front of a vacant lot at No. 241 West Sixty-second-st. the riot broke out. Some of the gang had climbed to the roof of No. 239, and a volley of bricks, wrenched from the chimneys, fell about the policeman.

In the first volley one of the bricks struck the policeman on the leg, and a shout of delight went up from the mob that encircled him. The cry brought other negroes from the tenement houses to the scene, and soon Connor found himself in a dangerous position.

Swinging his club, he backed his prisoner up to a high board fence in front of the vacant lot and faced the mob. Another shower of bricks from the roofs across the street fell about the policeman, some striking his assailants and others breaking windows at No. 239.

Connor blew his whistle, and a few moments later Policemen Kellaher and Downey arrived on a run from Amsterdam-ave. The mob instantly scattered and fled to the roofs, and soon the tops of the houses were lined with figures.

Turning his prisoner over to his comrades, Connor drew his revolver and fired at a negro on the roof of No. 239, who had hit him a second time with a brick. The negro ducked to safety, and the policeman started for the entrance of the house, determined to capture him.

Before he reached the entrance two negroes appeared at the front window of the top flat and fired at him. Their shots were answered by a white pedestrian, who was endeavoring to get through the mass of excited negroes. The stranger blazed away at the top flat until the temporary occupants disappeared, and the glass from the windows fell on the mob that pursued Connor to the extrance of the house.

About this time an excited mulatto dashed into the West Sixty-eighth-st. station. He shouted, "Killing a cop down in Sixty-second-st." and dashed out again before Sergeant Fitzpatrick could stop him.

Captain Kear and Sergeant Tierney, with the reserve of fourteen men in a patrol wagon, started for the scene. Meanwhile Policeman Connor had gained the roof of No. 239 and surprised William Brackett, a negro, of No. 222 West Sixty-seventh-st., in the act of throwing bricks on Kelleher and Downey, who were defending themselves against the gang in the street.

Dragging his prisoner to where his brother policemen were holding Johnson, Connor left Brackett, and, fighting his way through the crowd, cracking the head of every man who stood in his way, reached a patrol box at Amsterdam-ave. and turned in a call for reserves to Police Headquarters. The call was duplicated to the West Forty-seventh and West One-hundredth st. stations, and the reserves from each station were soon on the way to the scene, where they joined the Sixty-eighth-st. station men.

Captain Kear, on his arrival, succeeded in clearing the street and was pursuing the rioters to the roofs when the other reserves arrived in patrol wagons. In a few moments the policemen swarmed through the tenement houses looking for the rioters, but the latter had retreated to their homes, and peace appeared to be restored. But as the policemen assembled again in the street, a window in one of the houses went up and a negress emptied a pail of dirty water on the file of policemen. The water struck Policeman Cahill, of the West Sixty-eighth-st. station and drenched him to the skin. The woman could not be found.

Captain Kear put two men on each of the posts in the locality as a precautionary measure, fearing that the riot would break out afresh. The policemen asserted there would have been no riot if they had had their long night sticks.

POLICE BATTLE WITH BLACKS OVER ROOFS

Reserves Are Needed in New York to Quell a Race Riot.
NEW YORK, July 12.—A riot which required the reserves of three police precincts to suppress broke out tonight in the negro quarter in West Sixty-second street. The trouble was precipitated by the attempt of Policeman Connor to arrest William Johnson, the leader of a gang of negroes who were making a disturbance in the street.

The policeman secured his prisoner after a sharp fight and was dragging him to the station house when he was assailed by a mob and volleys of bricks and stones were hurled at him from the roofs of adjoining tenements.

On the arrival of two other policemen Connor opened fire on a negro on a roof and the shots were returned from the windows of the house. The reserves cleared the streets and chased the rioters over the roofs, making several arrests and finally restored order.

MANY COPS, NO RACE RIOT. Republicans Ask Police to Protect Negroes on the Big Block.
Because a crowd gathered after he had arrested a negro in the densely populated "Big Block," between West End and Amsterdam avenues in Sixty-second street, a policeman got excited last night and notified Police Headquarters that a "race riot" was on again. There was a muss in the same block on Sunday. In a Jiffy thirty policemen—the reserves from the West Forty-seventh and Sixty-eighth street stations Inspector Walsh, six of his men, and Capt. Kear of the West Sixty-eighth street station,—swarmed through the block.

They found no riot, but their arrival filled the street up with people from the houses. Some of the negroes became disturbed at the sight of so many blue uniforms and a delegation called at the Nineteenth Assembly district Republican Club, at Sixty-fifth street and Broadway, and asked the members to see that they were protected.

Ex-Collector George R. Bidwell, J. Van Vechten Olcott, Thomas P. Gilman and several other members of the club went to the West Sixty-eighth street station and told Sergt. Tierney that the negroes wanted protection. The sergeant said they would get it.

There wouldn't have been any trouble it seems if Patrick H. Harrington of 426 West Forty-eighth street, said to be the son of a former Alderman, hadn't gone into the "Big Block" to collect money for some one. He was held up by two negroes, he says, and hit on the head with a brick. He ran to the Sixty-eighth street station, and Policeman Kelly went back with him and arrested Charles Naething, 17 years old.

Of course a crowd gathered, and Kelly is said to have lost his head and sent for the reserves. It was said at Headquarters that a citizen telephoned a similar alarm. At any rate a lot of policemen were routed out of bed for nothing. Capt. Kear said angrily: "If Kelly did that, I'll give him a talking to. I don't know of any better way to start trouble in the neighborhood than to fire a lot of policemen into it."

RAGE RIOT IN NEW YORK
Negroes Who Beat a White Man Are Driven From the Streets.
New York, July 14.—Several negroes have been hurt in a resumption of the race rioting, which broke out in the vicinity of West Fifty-second street and Amsterdam avenue Sunday.

Several young colored men attacked and severely beat a son of Alderman Harrington to-day. Police hurried to the scene and made one arrest. On the way to the station they were assailed by showers of bricks. After the police dispersed the mob, every negro was assaulted and driven from the streets. Several were severely beaten.

THE COLOR A MARK.
Race Riots in New York—Lawlessness Condemned—A Colored Girl wins Honors—Delegates Return from Kentucky—The Negro Question—Notes.

New York, N. Y., Special.—It is passing strange that whenever a race riot occurs the Negroes seem to be the chief offenders and the only ones who invariably have to be clubbed and then arrested by the police. It is an unheard-of occurrence for a white man to be clubbed for attacking a Negro, and we wonder why it is vice versa.

On Saturday night there was a clash between the whites and blacks in 133d street, between Lenox and Ffth aves. Two white men and a boy got into an altercation with two or three Negroes. Politeman Michael Quinn was called to the assistance of the whites, and later when passing through the street, he, (Quinn), had some further trouble which could have been easily settled, but a number of white men became abusive and the Negroes resentful. Police captain Martens and twenty-one policemen were called out and hurried to the scene in a patrol wagon. They were just in time to avert a serious race war, for as it was, there were several hundred whites and Negroes in the street, scores of them fighting, and several pistol shots were heard. Seven Negroes are arrested, but there is no account of a single white man having been taken in custoddy.
